title: A meal in Bhubaneswar
lead: A meal in Bhubaneswar can lead from a pot of dalma to the sweets of Old Town. Ask how a dish is made, who makes it and where it belongs: the answers tell different parts of the city’s food story.
photo_context: Chhena poda photographed in Puri, 2022. A portrait of the dish, not a Bhubaneswar restaurant or a promised serving.

sections.title: Dalma: the pot and the finishing touch
sections.text: Dalma brings lentils and vegetables together, but the finishing spices matter too. The city’s published recipe cooks the lentils and vegetables, adds a separate tempering in ghee, then finishes with roasted cumin and dried chilli ground to a powder. It lists either toor or moong dal and vegetables such as brinjal, yam and cauliflower.
sections.question: “Which dal did you use, and what went into the tempering?”
paragraphs: This gives you two things to notice: what has softened together in the pot, and what has been added towards the end. Ask which vegetables were used and how the cook finishes the dalma. A recipe can explain a method without becoming a rule for every household or kitchen.

sections.title: Pakhala: ask what is in the bowl
sections.text: Pakhala starts with cooked rice and water, but that description leaves room for different preparations. The city’s recipe includes curd, ginger, green chilli and lemon, with an optional mustard-and-cumin tempering. The name alone therefore does not tell you whether the bowl contains dairy or how it has been seasoned.
sections.question: “How is today’s pakhala prepared, and what comes with it?”
paragraphs: Ask whether the kitchen is serving a fresh or fermented preparation, and which accompaniments come with it. Let that answer guide the rest of the order. Pakhala need not be treated as one more bowl alongside an already complete meal; you can make it the centre of lunch and choose the sides around it.

sections.title: Chhena poda: a sweet that keeps changing
sections.text: Chhena poda is a baked chhena sweet. In a 2021 account, Bhubaneswar chef Michael describes making a chocolate version for the city’s .FEST celebration. His recipe mixes chocolate into the chhena before baking. It is a specific example of a cook adapting an Odia sweet, rather than proof that every version follows one fixed formula.
sections.question: Compare the edge with the cut centre. What changes between the two?
paragraphs: The same account places the sweet’s beginnings in Nayagarh and retells the story of Sudarshana Sahoo leaving sweetened chhena in a warm oven. Read that as the origin story the chef recounts, not an independently established invention date. The documented modern adaptation is a different kind of evidence from the retrospective story.

The photograph here was taken in Puri. Its browned edges and pale cut surfaces give you something concrete to compare when you encounter the dish yourself. The fruit and garnish belong to this photographed serving; they do not define how chhena poda must be presented.

sections.title: Korakhai and the life of Old Town
sections.text: Old Town gives the meal a more local connection. The city’s Streets of Ekamra account places korakhai among sweets offered to deities in the neighbourhood and connects temple food with the cooks of Ananta Vasudev. Food here is part of worship and skilled work as well as something a visitor might buy.
paragraphs: In her 2016 report, Sheela Pattanayak describes korakhai made with khai, sugar or jaggery, coconut and cardamom. Temple sevak Trinath Badu tells her that designated confectioner families prepare the Lingaraj offering. Shop owner Subash Sahu describes customers buying the sweet for themselves as well as for offerings. These are named accounts from that report, not new interviews.

The distinction matters when you buy a packet: a sweet associated with a temple is not automatically a consecrated offering. Ask who made it and how it is intended to be used. The report preserves a moment in the city’s food trade; its shop details and prices cannot establish what is available today.
sections.question: “Is this made here, and is this packet intended as an offering or for eating at home?”

closing: Choose a kitchen according to the meal you want, then ask about ingredients, dietary requirements, portions and price. These food stories are starting points for a conversation, not a reviewed restaurant list or a current menu. In Old Town, check visiting and serving arrangements locally and give worshippers and cooks room to go about their work.
